options.t: The node runs from the start: the card is charged again.
options.why: Resume restarts the whole node. The code before the interrupt runs again.

options.t: Execution continues on the line after the interrupt.
options.why: It looks that way, but the runtime does not do that.

options.t: The whole graph runs again from START.
options.why: Only the interrupted node restarts. The earlier nodes are saved in the checkpoint.

options.t: It raises an error: interrupt cannot come after a side effect.
options.why: LangGraph does not detect this. The effect simply repeats.

questions.stem: The `agent` → `tools` loop uses 2 super-steps per iteration, and the run ends with one more `agent` step that answers. `recursion_limit` is 10. How many tool iterations can the agent run and still finish?

options.why: The limit counts super-steps: $2 \times 4 + 1 = 9 \le 10$. A fifth iteration needs $2 \times 5 + 1 = 11$.
5 iterations use all 10 super-steps; the final `agent` step is the 11th and raises `GraphRecursionError`.
The limit counts super-steps, not iterations. Each iteration has 2.

options.t: Unlimited, if there is an edge to END.
options.why: The edge to END helps only if the exit condition occurs before the limit.

questions.stem: The user comes back the next day, in a **new conversation**. The agent must remember that the user prefers short answers. Where must this live?

options.t: In the store, in a namespace for the user.
options.why: The store keeps memory across threads. A new conversation is another thread.
That reopens yesterday's full conversation, not a new conversation.

options.t: In the graph state, in a `preferences` key.
options.why: The state belongs to one thread. The new thread starts empty.
Then it applies to all users.

questions.stem: A node receives a list of $k$ documents, and $k$ is known only at run time. Each document must be summarized in parallel. What do you use?

options.t: `Send`: one per document, with a reducer to merge the summaries.
options.why: Send creates one branch per item, each with its own input. It is the LangGraph map-reduce.
Edges are fixed at compile time. $k$ exists only at run time.
Interrupt pauses for external input. It does not parallelize.
That is sequential, and a change to the limit does not create branches.

questions.stem: Key `msgs` with `operator.add` has the value `["a", "b"]`. You call `update_state(cfg, {"msgs": ["c"]})`. What is `msgs` in the new checkpoint?

options.why: `update_state` is treated as a node update: it goes through the reducer.
It overwrites only if the key has no reducer.
The old checkpoint stays intact, but a new one is created with the update applied.

options.t: Error: you cannot edit a key that has a reducer.
options.why: You can. The value only goes through the reducer.

questions.stem: A flow moves money. A checkpoint lost in a crash would be serious. Which durability mode do you choose?

options.why: It writes each checkpoint before the next step starts. It costs performance.
It writes in parallel with the next step. A crash can lose the last checkpoint.
It writes only at the end. A crash mid-run loses everything since the start.

options.t: None: the checkpointer already guarantees this.
options.why: The mode sets when the write happens. The risk depends on it.

questions.stem: Explain what a super-step is and when the node updates take effect.
questions.answer: A super-step is one tick of the graph: all nodes scheduled for that tick run, in parallel if there is more than one. The reducers of each key apply the updates only at the end of the tick. So a node does not see the update of another node in the same tick. The checkpoint is saved at each super-step, and the recursion limit counts super-steps.

questions.stem: Explain how `interrupt()` works, what it requires and how to write the node so that side effects do not repeat.
questions.answer: `interrupt(value)` pauses the graph inside the node and returns the value to the caller. It requires a checkpointer and a `thread_id`. Resume is `Command(resume=x)` on the same thread, and `x` becomes the return value of `interrupt()`. The node restarts from the first line, so everything before the interrupt runs again. So put the interrupt at the start of the node, or in a dedicated node, and put the side effect after it or in another node.

d1-01-hedge-fisico.title: Cost of the physical hedge
d1-01-hedge-fisico.source: Lecture notes (Learn Anything, Delta One); illustrative numbers, not from any real desk
d1-01-hedge-fisico.intro:
Student notes. One example runs to the end: the client goes **long a TRS of 10 million USD** on a stock and pays SOFR + 50 bp. The desk buys the stock to hedge.
Question of the note: do these 50 bp pay for the hedge? All numbers are illustrative.

objectives.text: why only the spreads over SOFR matter, and who charges each cost line
the funding cost of a position with repo and haircut
the leverage charge (SLR), and explain $K_e$ minus debt
the P&L of the cost stack and the break-even
the effect of a stock going special and the risks of securities lending

sections.title: 1. The scenario and the unit
sections.body:
- Client long TRS: receives the stock return, pays SOFR + spread.
- Desk: is short the return → buys the stock (physical hedge) → needs cash to carry the position.
- The client pays SOFR. The desk pays SOFR for its funding. **SOFR cancels.**
- Only the spreads over SOFR remain. Unit for everything: **bp per year on the notional**.
- Conversion: 1 bp on 10 million = 1,000 USD per year.
- Consequence: if SOFR rises or falls, the funding carry does not change. (The leverage line uses all-in $K_e - K_d$; it stays the same only if $K_e$ moves with rates.)

sections.title: 2. Funding: repo + haircut
sections.body:
- Treasury (ALM) funds the desk inventory and charges an internal price: the **FTP**.
- The FTP covers the bank's cost of debt and the use of scarce balance sheet.
- The stock goes into a **repo**: secured funding, cheap. But the repo does not fund 100%.
- **Haircut** = the part that the repo does not cover. It is funded unsecured, at a higher cost.
- Example: 10 million, haircut of 15%.
  1. 8.5 million in repo, at SOFR + 30 bp.
  2. 1.5 million unsecured, at SOFR + 100 bp.
  3. Cost = $0.85 \times 30 + 0.15 \times 100$ = 25.5 + 15 = **40.5 bp**.
- The haircut is the weight in the mix. Higher haircut → more expensive funding.
- The unsecured spread is the bank's own credit spread. It increases with the term.
- Term funding costs more than overnight. Funding a 1-year swap overnight is cheap, but it carries rollover risk.

sections.title: 3. Leverage (SLR)
sections.body:
- SLR = Tier 1 capital / total leverage exposure.
- The exposure counts **every asset at full size**, with no risk weight. 10 million of a liquid, safe stock weighs the same as 10 million of a risky one.
- Idea: a fraction of the asset must be funded with equity instead of debt. Equity requires a higher return.
$$\text{charge} = E \times L \times (K_e - K_d)$$
- $E$ = exposure (% of notional); $L$ = leverage requirement; $K_e$ = cost of equity; $K_d$ = cost of debt.
- Why $K_e$ **minus** debt: the funding lines already charged the cost of debt on 100% of the asset. Equity only replaces a part of that debt. A full $K_e$ charge counts the debt twice.
- Example: physical stock (exposure 100%), requirement 4.5%, $K_e$ 12%, debt 5%.
  1. Excess: 12% − 5% = 7%.
  2. Charge: $100\% \times 4.5\% \times 7\%$ = **31.5 bp**.
- In this example it is the largest single line (funding is split into repo 25.5 and haircut 15).
- US eSLR rule (in force since 1 Apr 2026, for G-SIB holding companies): it moved from 3% + a fixed 2% to 3% + half of the G-SIB surcharge. The requirement fell.
- Effect of 5% → 4.5%: 35 bp → 31.5 bp. 3.5 bp less per year.

sections.title: 4. Counterparty capital
sections.body:
- It is a different constraint, on a different thing: the risk that the **client** defaults on the swap.
- Base: risk-weighted exposure (RWA). It depends on the client, the margin and the term.
- Leverage vs counterparty capital:
  1. Leverage: size of the asset, no risk weight.
  2. Counterparty capital: credit risk of the client, with risk weight.
- The two are usually charged in separate lines. In the example: **10 bp**.

sections.title: 5. Securities lending: the negative line
sections.body:
- The desk is long the stock. Prime Brokerage / Sec Lending lends this stock to short sellers and charges a fee. The desk receives a share. It is **revenue**: a negative cost.
- **GC** (general collateral): easy to borrow. Fee from a few bp up to about 30 bp per year.
- **Special**: scarce supply or high short demand. The fee goes to hundreds or thousands of bp.
- Utilization = shares on loan / lendable supply. High → little slack → the fee can jump. It leads the fee.
- Days to cover = short interest / average daily volume. High → squeeze risk and a candidate for special.
- Rebate (cash collateral) = reinvestment rate − borrow fee.
  1. GC: 4.30% − 0.25% = 4.05%.
  2. Special: 4.30% − 6% = **−1.70%**. Negative rebate: the borrower pays on top.
- Recall: the lender asks for the shares back. The borrower returns them, borrows from another lender, or suffers a **buy-in** (purchase in the market, at the borrower's cost).
- In the example, GC stock: the desk receives **10 bp**.

sections.title: 6. The stack and the P&L
sections.body:
- The five lines of the physical hedge:
  1. Repo: 25.5
  2. Unsecured haircut: 15
  3. Leverage: 31.5
  4. Counterparty capital: 10
  5. Securities lending: −10
- Total cost = **72 bp**.
- P&L = 50 − 72 = **−22 bp** ≈ −22,000 USD per year on 10 million.
- Conclusion: 50 bp do not pay for a standalone physical hedge on a GC stock.
- Same case, but the stock goes special: fee of 300 bp, the desk keeps half.
  1. Lending: −150 instead of −10.
  2. Cost = 82 − 150 = **−68 bp** (net revenue).
  3. P&L = 50 + 68 = **+118 bp** ≈ +118,000 USD per year.
- On a special, the long hedge pays for itself. The client spread is fixed, and the desk keeps the extra.

sections.title: 7. Decision rule
sections.body:
- The physical hedge makes a profit when: **client spread ≥ funding + leverage + capital − lending**.
- Break-even in the example: cost without lending = 82 bp. With the client at 50, the desk needs 32 bp of lending revenue. With half the fee, that is a borrow fee of **64 bp**.
- If the numbers do not work: internalize against another client's short, or do the synthetic hedge (next note).

sections.title: 8. Where I get confused
sections.body:
- SOFR is not in the calculation. Only spreads.
- The haircut is the **weight** of the expensive funding, not a cost in bp.
- Leverage uses $K_e$ − debt. A full $K_e$ counts the debt twice.
- Leverage has no risk weight. Counterparty capital has one. They are different lines.
- Securities lending is revenue for whoever is **long** the stock. For whoever is short, special is a cost.
- The desk receives a **share** of the borrow fee, not the full fee.
- Negative rebate exists: borrow fee above the reinvestment rate.
- bp on notional → dollars: 1 bp on 10 million = 1,000 USD per year.

d1-01-hedge-fisico.summary:
### Unit
- SOFR cancels. Everything in bp/year on the notional. 1 bp on 10 million = 1,000 USD/year.
### The lines (funding = repo + haircut)
- Funding = $(1-h) \times \text{repo} + h \times \text{unsecured}$. E.g.: $0.85 \times 30 + 0.15 \times 100$ = 40.5.
- Leverage = exposure × requirement × ($K_e$ − debt). E.g.: $100\% \times 4.5\% \times 7\%$ = 31.5.
- Counterparty capital: client risk, by RWA. E.g.: 10.
- Securities lending: revenue. GC ≈ −10; special = hundreds of bp.
### P&L
- Cost = 40.5 + 31.5 + 10 − 10 = 72. Client 50 → −22 bp.
- Special (300 bp, half to the desk): cost −68 → +118 bp.
### Rule
- Profit if spread ≥ funding + leverage + capital − lending.
- Otherwise: internalize or synthetic hedge.
### Sec lending
- Rebate = reinvestment − borrow fee (can be negative).
- Signals: utilization and days to cover rising; recalls.

questions.stem: Repo at SOFR + 20 bp, unsecured funding at SOFR + 120 bp, haircut of 10%. What is the funding cost?

options.why: That is the simple average of the two rates. The weight of the expensive funding is the haircut: 10%.
This ignores the haircut. The repo does not fund 100% of the position.
This adds the two rates. A mix funds the position, not both rates in full.

questions.stem: Physical stock, leverage requirement of 5%, $K_e$ of 13%, cost of debt of 5%. What is the leverage charge?

options.why: This uses the full $K_e$ ($5\% \times 13\%$). The funding lines already charged the debt.
This uses only the cost of debt ($5\% \times 5\%$). The charge is on the excess cost of equity.
That is the excess $K_e$ − debt, in %, read as bp. It still needs the multiplication by the 5% requirement.

questions.stem: Why does the leverage charge use $K_e$ minus the cost of debt, and not the full $K_e$?

options.t: Because equity replaces debt that the funding lines already charged.
options.why: Funding was charged on 100% of the asset. To replace a slice with equity costs only the difference between equity and debt.

options.t: Because the regulator requires the deduction of debt.
options.why: It is an internal pricing convention, so that the same cost is not counted twice.

options.t: Because the stock is a liquid asset.
options.why: Liquidity does not matter here: the SLR has no risk weight.

options.t: Because the client pays SOFR, which cancels the debt.
options.why: SOFR cancels between the client leg and the funding lines. In the leverage line, $K_e$ and $K_d$ are both all-in rates (12% and 5%); the excess that equity demands does not cancel.

questions.stem: Stack: funding 30, leverage 40, capital 8, lending −12. The client pays SOFR + 60. What is the desk's annual P&L on a notional of 20 million?

options.why: The sign is wrong: the cost (66) is greater than the spread (60).
This forgets the lending revenue (cost of 78 instead of 66).
That is for 10 million. The notional is 20 million.

questions.stem: Same stack (cost of 78 bp before lending, client at 60 bp). The desk keeps half of the borrow fee. Which borrow fee makes the P&L zero?

options.why: The desk needs 78 − 60 = 18 bp of revenue. With half the fee: borrow fee of 36 bp.
18 bp is the necessary revenue. The desk receives only half of the borrow fee.
This divides by 2 instead of multiplying.
This covers the full cost alone, without the client's 60 bp.

questions.stem: Cash collateral earns 4.00%. The borrow fee of the stock is 5.50%. What is the borrower's rebate?

options.why: Rebate = 4.00% − 5.50% = −1.50%. The borrower gives up the interest and also pays 1.50%.
The sign is wrong: the borrow fee is greater than the reinvestment rate.

options.t: 0%: the rebate does not go negative.
options.why: It does. That is the mark of a special stock.
This ignores the borrow fee.

questions.stem: SOFR falls from 4.30% to 3.80%. What happens to the desk's funding carry (client financing leg vs hedge funding) on a client long TRS with a physical hedge?

options.t: Nothing: SOFR cancels on both legs.
options.why: The desk receives SOFR from the client and pays SOFR on the funding. Only the spreads remain.

options.t: It improves, because funding gets cheaper.
options.why: Funding falls, but what the desk receives from the client falls by the same amount.

options.t: It gets worse, because the client pays less.
options.why: The client pays less, but the desk's funding falls by the same amount.
The haircut changes the funding spread, not the exposure to the SOFR level.

questions.stem: The desk is long the stock as a hedge of a client long TRS, with a fixed spread. The stock goes special. What is the effect for the desk?

options.t: It improves: lending revenue rises and the client spread stays the same.
options.why: The holder of the stock can lend it at a high fee. The client continues to pay the contracted spread.

options.t: It gets worse: the desk starts to pay the borrow fee.
options.why: Whoever is short and must borrow the stock pays the fee.

options.t: Nothing changes: the gain passes to the client.
options.why: The spread is fixed in the contract. The pass-through is not automatic.

options.t: It gets worse: the repo haircut rises.
options.why: Special is about scarcity in securities lending. It does not set the haircut.

questions.stem: Why do 10 million of a liquid, safe stock use so much balance sheet at a G-SIB bank?

options.t: Because the SLR counts the asset at full size, with no risk weight.
options.why: For leverage, only size matters. The risk of the stock does not reduce the exposure.

options.t: Because liquid stocks have a larger haircut.
options.why: The opposite is true: liquid stocks have a smaller haircut.

options.t: Because counterparty capital is larger for liquid stocks.
options.why: Counterparty capital depends on the swap client, not on the liquidity of the stock.

options.t: Because GC stocks generate no lending revenue.
options.why: They generate a little, but that is a different line. The question is about balance sheet.

questions.stem: List the five cost lines of a physical hedge. For each, say in one sentence what it charges.
questions.answer: 1) Repo: secured funding of most of the position. 2) Haircut: the part that the repo does not cover, funded unsecured, at a higher cost. 3) Leverage (SLR): the excess return of equity over debt, on the fraction of the asset that requires capital. 4) Counterparty capital: the credit risk of the client on the swap. 5) Securities lending: revenue, with a negative sign.

questions.stem: Explain GC and special, and give two signals that a stock can go special.
questions.answer: GC is a stock that is easy to borrow, with a fee of a few bp. Special is a stock that is scarce or in high demand from short sellers, with a fee of hundreds of bp. Signals: rising utilization (little free supply), rising fee or falling rebate, recalls, high days to cover, and events such as M&A or index deletion.

d1-02-hedge-sintetico.title: Synthetic hedge and switches
d1-02-hedge-sintetico.source: Lecture notes (Learn Anything, Delta One); illustrative numbers, not from any real desk
d1-02-hedge-sintetico.intro:
This note continues the physical hedge note. Same client: long TRS of 10 million, pays SOFR + 50 bp. The physical hedge cost **72 bp** and gave −22 bp.
Question of the note: is there a cheaper route, and when is a switch worth it? All numbers are illustrative.

objectives.text: the hedge routes of a TRS and the order in which you check each one
the all-in cost of a synthetic hedge, with the reduced leverage
the financing rate and the borrow implied in option prices
whether a switch between physical and synthetic pays off
the borrow risk in a client short swap

sections.title: 1. The hedge routes
sections.body:
- For a client long TRS on a stock, the routes:
  1. **Internalize** against another client's short.
  2. Buy the stock (physical).
  3. Swap with a street dealer (swap facility).
  4. Listed options: long call + short put.
- For an index, there is also the future.
- Order: check internalization first. Rank the others by all-in cost (section 8); the cheapest changes with the inputs.
- Why internalization comes first: a client long against a client short needs no hedge, no stock and no balance sheet. Cost near zero, and the desk earns the spread on both sides.

sections.title: 2. Why the synthetic uses less balance sheet
sections.body:
- Physical stock: enters the leverage exposure at **100%** of the notional.
- Derivative: enters at replacement cost + a potential future exposure add-on (SA-CCR). For a 1-year margined swap, about **15%**.
- Same formula as the previous note:
  1. Physical: $100\% \times 4.5\% \times 7\%$ = 31.5 bp.
  2. Synthetic: $15\% \times 4.5\% \times 7\%$ ≈ **4.7 bp**.
- The largest line of the physical hedge falls to almost nothing. It is the main reason to go synthetic.

sections.title: 3. Swap with a dealer
sections.body:
- The desk goes long a swap with another bank. The dealer carries the stock.
- Why the dealer can quote below your physical cost:
  1. Cheaper funding or balance sheet than yours.
  2. The dealer matches your trade with flow from its own clients.
- The dealer spread is **your funding cost**. Add your own leverage and capital lines.
- Example: the dealer charges SOFR + 29.
  1. Dealer spread: 29
  2. Your leverage (15%): 4.7
  3. Your counterparty capital: client 10 (same as in the physical hedge) + dealer 2 = 12
- All-in = **45.7 bp**. P&L = 50 − 45.7 = **+4.3 bp**.
- The physical hedge gave −22. The route changed the sign of the trade.
- What you lose: the securities lending revenue. The dealer now holds the stock.

sections.title: 4. Synthetic forward with options
sections.body:
- Long call + short put, same strike and expiry = **long synthetic forward**.
- (Long put + short call = **short** synthetic.)
- The premium is **not** the cost: it buys an asset that is worth what it cost.
- The cost is the **implied financing rate** in the prices, compared with your funding.
- Put-call parity with dividends:
$$C - P = S - PV(\text{div}) - K \cdot DF(T)$$
- Intuition: the combination is the stock with deferred payment. You solve for $DF(T)$.
- Example: $S = 100$, $K = 100$, 1 year, no dividends, $C - P = 4.60$.
  1. $K \cdot DF = 100 - 4.60 = 95.40$ → $DF = 0.954$.
  2. Implied rate = $1/0.954 - 1$ = **4.82%**.
  3. With SOFR at 4.30%: implied spread of 52 bp.
- Compare these 52 bp with the other routes. Add your leverage and the execution cost.

sections.title: 5. What options tell you about borrow
sections.body:
- Hard-to-borrow stock: short sellers cannot find the stock, so they sell the synthetic forward.
- The implied forward falls **below** the theoretical forward. The difference is the borrow fee.
- Example: $S = 100$, rate 4.30%, 1 year, no dividends.
  1. Theoretical forward: 104.30.
  2. Forward implied by the options: 101.30.
  3. Difference: 3.00 → borrow of ≈ **300 bp**.
- Use: it is a market signal that the stock is special, before the fee appears on your stock loan screen.
- For a desk long through a physical hedge, special is good: the desk lends the stock at a high fee, and the client spread is fixed.

sections.title: 6. Switch: change the route without changing the delta
sections.body:
- Switch = move the hedge between physical and synthetic, with the same delta before and after.
- Three reasons:
  1. The stock goes special → go physical and earn the lending fee.
  2. Balance sheet pressure (reporting dates) → go synthetic.
  3. The relative cost of the routes changes.
- Execution without market risk: both legs in a **package**, at a single price.
  1. Dealer: sell the stock and enter the swap at the same price.
  2. Options: to go synthetic, a reversal (sell the stock, buy a call, sell a put); to go physical, a conversion (buy the stock, buy a put, sell a call).
  3. Index: EFP.
- Conversion = long stock + long put + short call. Reversal = short stock + long call + short put.
- Worth it when: savings over the remaining term > bid-ask of the two legs.
- Example: savings of 72 − 45.7 = 26.3 bp per year. Switch cost: 8 bp.
  1. 6 months remain: 26.3 × 0.5 = 13.2 bp > 8 → **do it**.
  2. 3 months remain: 26.3 × 0.25 = 6.6 bp < 8 → **do not do it**.

sections.title: 7. Client short: the borrow risk
sections.body:
- Client short TRS: receives SOFR − spread on the financing leg. The spread covers the borrow fee that the desk pays.
- On a special stock, the spread can exceed SOFR: the client pays.
- The desk is short the stock → it must borrow the stock.
- **Term mismatch**: the client spread is fixed for the term of the swap. The borrow fee floats every day, and the lender can recall.
- Term liability, overnight funding. If the fee jumps, the desk loses.
- Four defenses:
  1. Term borrow (locks the fee, costs a premium).
  2. Right to reprice, in the confirm.
  3. ISDA events: increased cost or loss of stock borrow.
  4. Price buffer on high-utilization stocks.
- Signals that the stock will go special: rising utilization, rising fee, recalls, events (M&A, convertible, index deletion), implied forward below the theoretical forward.

sections.title: 8. Decision rule
sections.body:
- All-in cost of each route: **spread + $E \times L \times (K_e - K_d)$ + capital − lending + execution**.
- Choose the lowest. Recalculate when an input changes: borrow fee, dealer quote, balance sheet pressure.
- In the example: internalize ≈ 0 › dealer 45.7 › physical 72.

sections.title: 9. Where I get confused
sections.body:
- The dealer spread is not the full cost. Your leverage and your capital are missing.
- In the synthetic, the desk **loses** the securities lending revenue.
- The option premium is not a cost. The cost is the implied rate.
- Hedge of a client long = long call + short put. It is easy to invert.
- Implied forward **below** the theoretical forward = stock expensive to borrow, not cheap.
- Switch savings are per year. Multiply by the remaining term before you compare them with the cost.
- Special helps the desk that is long physical and hurts the desk that is short. The sign depends on the side.

d1-02-hedge-sintetico.summary:
### Routes (client long)
- Internalize first. Then the cheapest all-in of: physical, swap with dealer, call − put. Index: future.
### Balance sheet
- Physical: exposure 100% → 31.5 bp. Margined swap: ≈ 15% → 4.7 bp.
### All-in
- spread + exposure × lev. × ($K_e$ − debt) + capital − lending + execution.
- Dealer: 29 + 4.7 + 12 = 45.7 → +4.3 bp. Physical: 72 → −22 bp.
### Options
$$C - P = S - PV(\text{div}) - K \cdot DF(T)$$
- Solve for $DF$ → implied rate. The premium is not a cost.
- Implied forward below the theoretical forward → the difference is the borrow.
### Switch
- Do it if savings × remaining term > bid-ask of the two legs. As a package (dealer, reversal or conversion, EFP).
### Client short
- Fixed spread × floating borrow fee + recall = term mismatch.
- Defenses: term borrow, repricing, ISDA events, buffer.

questions.stem: Margined swap: exposure of 20%, leverage requirement of 5%, $K_e$ − debt of 8%. What is the leverage charge?

options.why: That is the physical hedge, with exposure of 100%.
That is $20\% \times 8\%$. It still needs the multiplication by the 5% requirement.
This applies the 20% exposure twice.

questions.stem: The dealer quotes SOFR + 30. Your lines: leverage 8, capital 5. The client pays SOFR + 60. What is the P&L of the synthetic route?

options.why: This uses only the dealer spread. Your leverage and your capital are missing.
This leaves out your leverage line: 60 − (30 + 5). The dealer swap still uses some balance sheet: 8 bp.
This subtracts only your lines and forgets the dealer spread.

questions.stem: $S = 50$, $K = 50$, 1 year, no dividends, $C - P = 2.50$. What is the implied financing rate (simple interest)?

options.why: That is $2.50/50$: the discount on the future value. The rate is on the present value, 47.50.
This reads $C - P$ directly as a rate.
That is $0.05/1.05$: the calculation in the wrong direction.

questions.stem: Why is the premium paid for the synthetic forward (call − put) not the cost of the hedge?

options.t: Because the premium buys an asset worth that price. The cost is the implied rate, against your funding.
options.why: The combination is equivalent to the stock with deferred payment. What you pay for the deferral is the embedded rate.

options.t: Because the call premium and the put premium always cancel.
options.why: They cancel only when the strike equals the forward.

options.t: Because listed options have no financing cost.
options.why: They have one: it is embedded in the difference $C - P$.

options.t: Because the premium is returned at expiry.
options.why: It is not returned. It becomes the value of the position.

questions.stem: The desk has a client long 10 million in a stock. Another client wants to be short 10 million in the same stock, through a swap. What is the best route?

options.t: Internalize: one swap hedges the other.
options.why: It needs no stock, no borrow and no balance sheet. The desk earns the spread on both sides.

options.t: Buy the stock for one client and borrow it for the other.
options.why: This uses balance sheet and pays a borrow fee with no need.

options.t: Do both hedges with a dealer.
options.why: It pays two spreads to the street for positions that offset each other.
It pays execution and an implied rate for a risk that is already flat.

questions.stem: A switch saves 30 bp per year. 4 months of the swap remain. The cost of the two legs is 12 bp. Is it worth it?

options.t: No: the savings over the term are 10 bp, less than 12.
options.why: $30 \times 4/12 = 10$ bp. The cost of 12 bp does not pay off.

options.t: Yes: 30 bp is more than 12 bp.
options.why: 30 bp is per year. Only 4 months remain.

options.t: Yes: the savings over the term are 120 bp.
options.why: This multiplies by 4 instead of by 4/12.
The savings over the term are 10 bp, not 12.

questions.stem: Client short swap, 1 year, fixed spread. The desk borrows the stock overnight. The borrow fee jumps from 50 to 400 bp. If the confirm has no repricing, who loses?

options.t: The desk: the cost floated, and the client revenue is fixed.
options.why: It is the term mismatch: a 1-year liability funded with an overnight borrow.

options.t: The client: the client pays the borrow fee of the day.
options.why: The client spread is fixed for the term of the swap.
The lender gains: the lender receives the higher fee.
SOFR cancels the base rate. The borrow fee is a spread and does not cancel.

questions.stem: $S = 100$, 1 year, no dividends. Theoretical forward: 104. Forward implied by the options: 102. What does this indicate?

options.t: Borrow of about 200 bp: the stock is expensive to borrow.
options.why: Short sellers who cannot find the stock sell the synthetic forward and push the price down. The difference of 2 on 100 is the borrow fee.

options.t: The stock is cheap to finance for short sellers.
options.why: The opposite is true: short sellers pay a high fee.
A dividend of about 2 would explain the gap, but the stem says there are no dividends.

options.t: Pricing error: the two must be equal.
options.why: They are equal only if the stock can be borrowed at no cost.

questions.stem: To hedge a client long TRS with options, which combination does the desk build?

options.t: Long call + short put, same strike and expiry.
options.why: It is the long synthetic forward: it gains when the stock rises, as the desk needs.
That is the short synthetic. It doubles the risk instead of hedging it.
That is a straddle: a volatility position, not delta one.
Short straddle: volatility risk, without the necessary delta.

questions.stem: Explain why a synthetic hedge uses less balance sheet than the physical hedge, and what the desk loses when it goes synthetic.
questions.answer: The physical stock enters the SLR leverage exposure at 100% of the notional. A derivative enters at replacement cost plus a potential future exposure add-on (SA-CCR), about 15% for a 1-year margined swap. The leverage charge falls from 31.5 to about 4.7 bp. What you lose: the securities lending revenue, because the dealer now holds the stock.

questions.stem: What is a switch, what are three reasons to do one, and how do you execute it without market risk?
questions.answer: A switch moves the hedge between physical and synthetic without a change in delta. Reasons: the stock went special (go physical and earn the lending fee), balance sheet pressure on reporting dates (go synthetic), and a change in relative cost. Execution: both legs in a package at a single price, through a dealer, a reversal or conversion with options, or an EFP on an index. It is worth it when the savings over the remaining term exceed the bid-ask of the two legs.

d1-05-produtos-precos.intro:
Student notes. The running example: the **USD 10 million TRS**, SOFR at 4.30%, spread of 50 bp.
This note covers the product math: the financing leg, the forward with a dividend, and what a future reveals.

the financing leg payment
the price of an equity forward with a dividend
the financing and the dividends implied in a future, and decide the trade
TRS, future, TRF and EFP; price return and total return

sections.title: 1. What delta one is
sections.body:
- Delta one = **linear** payoff in the underlying. Delta ≈ 1, no optionality.
- Products: TRS, forward, future, ETF, the stock itself.
- All deliver the same exposure. What changes: who finances, who keeps the dividend, where the counterparty risk sits, and how much balance sheet it uses.
- So the price of a delta one product is a price of **financing and dividends**, not of volatility.

sections.title: 2. The two legs of a TRS
sections.body:
- **Equity leg**: price return + dividends × DPR.
- **Financing leg**: notional × (benchmark + spread) × year fraction.
- Long client: **receives** the equity leg and **pays** the financing leg.
- Financing leg math:
$$\text{payment} = N \times (r + s) \times \frac{\text{days}}{360}$$
- Example: 10 million, SOFR 4.30%, spread 50 bp, 91 days, Act/360.
  1. Rate: 4.30% + 0.50% = 4.80%.
  2. Fraction: 91/360 = 0.2528.
  3. Payment ≈ **USD 121,333**.
- The spread is what the desk earns above SOFR: $10\,\text{m} \times 0.50\% \times 91/360$ ≈ USD 12.6k in the quarter. It must first pay the desk's funding and borrow cost above SOFR; only the rest is margin.

sections.title: 3. Resets and initial margin
sections.body:
- **Reset**: on each date, the swap settles the MTM and the notional goes back to market value.
- Purpose: it cuts the counterparty exposure and keeps the financing on the current notional.
- Two types:
  1. **Fixed quantity**: the number of shares does not change; the notional follows the price.
  2. **Fixed notional**: the number of shares changes to keep the notional. The hedge must **trade** at each reset.
- Fixed notional example: the stock rises 10%. At the reset, the desk sells about 9% of the shares to go back to 10 million.
- **Independent amount** (initial margin): collateral the client posts at inception, for example 10% to 20% of notional.
- It covers the price move until the desk can close out, and it sets the client's leverage: 20% → 5×.

sections.title: 4. Equity forward with a dividend
sections.body:
- Idea: buying the stock today and carrying it to $T$ costs financing and earns the dividend. The forward must break even with this.
$$F = S(1 + rT) - D\,(1 + r\,(T - t_D))$$
- Reading: you pay interest on the stock and do **not** receive the dividend. The dividend is taken to future value, from $t_D$ to $T$.
- Example: $S = 50$, $r = 5\%$, $T$ = 1 year, dividend of 2 in 6 months.
  1. Financed stock: $50 \times 1.05 = 52.50$.
  2. Dividend at future value: $2 \times 1.025 = 2.05$.
  3. $F = 52.50 - 2.05$ = **50.45**.
- With a continuous yield: $F = S\,e^{(r-q)T}$.
- Signs: higher rate → higher forward. Higher dividend → **lower** forward.

sections.title: 5. What a future reveals
sections.body:
- The same equation has three unknowns: price, financing and dividends. The future gives the price. If you know one of the other two, you extract the missing one.
- **Implied financing** (known dividends):
$$r = \frac{(F + D)/S - 1}{T}$$
- Example: index 5000, dividends of 20 points, 3-month future at 5050.
  1. $(5050 + 20)/5000 - 1 = 1.40\%$ for the quarter.
  2. Annualized: $1.40\% / 0.25$ = **5.6%**.
  3. Your funding is 5.3% → the future is **rich** by 30 bp.
  4. Trade: buy the basket and sell the future (cash-and-carry), if the 30 bp pay the costs.
- **Implied dividends** (known financing): $D = S(1 + rT) - F$.
- Example: index 5000, 5%, 3-month future at 5040 → $5062.5 - 5040$ = **22.5 points**.
- **Roll**: the spread between the front contract and the next one. It prices financing minus dividends of the next period. Rich roll = the market pays more for synthetic long exposure.
- **TRF** (total return future): listed future whose traded price is the **financing spread**. A cleared alternative to an index TRS.
- **EFP**: negotiated exchange of a future for a basket, at an agreed basis. It lets you switch route without market risk.

sections.title: 6. What a TRS is worth
sections.body:
- At inception, with zero spread, no dividends and a single curve: the TRS is worth ≈ **0**.
- Reason: under the risk-neutral measure, the expected total return of the stock is the risk-free rate. The equity leg and the floating leg have the same value.
- So the day-one value is the **PV of the spread**.
- Example: 10 million, 1 year, quarterly, flat curve at 4.3%, spread of 50 bp.
  1. Spread per quarter: 50 bp × 10 million × 91.25/360 (Act/360) ≈ USD 12.67k, so ≈ USD 50.7k per year.
  2. Discounted at 4.3%: ≈ **USD 49.4k** for the desk (−49.4k for the client).
  3. Without Act/360 (12.5k per quarter), the result would be ≈ 48.7k. The day count is worth ≈ 0.7k here.
- FinancePy's `EquitySwap.value` needs three curves:
  1. Discount: PV of the cash flows (collateral rate).
  2. Index: projects the floating rate.
  3. Dividends: set the equity forward.
- Which rate drives the equity forward on the desk: the stock's **repo/funding** rate, not OIS. It is the real cost to carry the hedge. The difference between the two is why the client pays a spread.

sections.title: 7. Why the client uses a swap
sections.body:
- Four reasons:
  1. Leverage without a margin loan.
  2. Market access without local custody or settlement.
  3. Easy short.
  4. One master agreement for many lines.
- What the client gives up: the vote. The client also takes on counterparty risk and tax rules (§871(m) on US stocks).
- **Price return vs total return**: price return pays only the price change. The client gives up the dividend, so the price compensates (lower financing or a forward-like level). Total return passes the dividend through via the DPR.
- **Cash PB vs synthetic prime**: in cash PB the client owns the stock, with a margin loan. In synthetic the client holds swaps, and the bank owns the hedges. Same economics; different balance sheet, legal and tax treatment.
- **Breakage**: the client terminates a 1-year swap in month 3. The desk may have locked term funding or borrow. The confirm usually sets an exit fee or a minimum term.

sections.title: 8. Where I get confused
sections.body:
- Long client **pays** financing and **receives** the equity leg. Do not invert.
- Act/360: 91 days is 91/360, not exactly 0.25 and not 91/365.
- In the forward, take the dividend to **future** value (from $t_D$ to $T$) before you subtract it.
- Higher dividend → lower forward.
- Implied financing: add $D$ to the future **before** you divide by $S$. Then annualize: divide by $T$.
- Rich future (implied > your funding) → sell the future and buy the basket. Cheap future → the opposite.
- Fixed notional requires trading at the reset. Fixed quantity does not.
- In a TRF, the traded quantity is the spread, not the index level.

d1-03-dividendos.title: Dividends, tax and indices
d1-03-dividendos.source: IRS Notice 2026-61 and Treas. Reg. §1.871-15; lecture notes (Learn Anything, Delta One). Illustrative numbers. Not tax advice
d1-03-dividendos.intro:
Student notes. The running example: a TRS on a **foreign stock that pays a dividend of 2.00**, with 15% tax withheld at source.
Question of the note: who keeps the dividend, who pays the tax, and where the desk makes or loses money.

sections.title: 1. The three dates
sections.body:
- **Ex-date**: decides who receives. Who holds the stock **before** it receives the dividend.
- **Record date**: the date of the shareholder register. The ex-date is set from it, because of settlement:
  1. **US** (T+1 since 28 May 2024): the ex-date is normally the **same day** as the record date.
  2. **T+2 markets** (e.g. most of Europe): the record date is the business day **after** the ex-date.
- **Pay date**: the day the cash arrives.
- On the ex-date, the price falls by roughly the dividend amount. The value left the stock and became cash receivable.
- In a swap: the confirm usually fixes the dividend amount on the ex-date and pays on the pay date. Check the confirm.
- Example: bought on the ex-date → does not receive the 2.00, but paid about 2.00 less.

sections.title: 2. DPR and the desk's dividend risk
sections.body:
- **DPR** (dividend pass-through ratio) = the fraction of the gross dividend that the swap passes to the client. E.g.: 100%, 85%, 70%.
- The desk holds the stock as a hedge. It **receives** the dividend net of tax and **pays** the dividend × DPR.
$$\text{P\&L} = D \times (1 - t) - D \times \text{DPR}$$
- $t$ = the tax the desk actually suffers at source.
- Example: $D = 2.00$, $t = 15\%$, DPR of 100%.
  1. Receives: $2.00 \times 85\% = 1.70$.
  2. Pays: 2.00.
  3. P&L: **−0.30 per share**. On 1 million shares: −300k.
- Fixes: DPR equal to the net rate (85%), or put the difference in the spread.
- The opposite also exists: DPR of 85% and the desk suffers only 10% → receives 1.80, pays 1.70 → **+0.10 per share**.

sections.title: 3. PR, GTR and NTR indices
sections.body:
- **PR** (price return): price only. The dividend drops out of the index.
- **GTR** (gross total return): reinvests the **gross** dividend.
- **NTR** (net total return): reinvests the net dividend, at the **index provider's standard** tax rate.
- The provider's rate is a convention. Each investor's real rate can differ (treaty, structure).
- Gain in an NTR swap: if the desk suffers less tax than the provider's rate, the difference is left over.
- Example: provider assumes 30%, the desk suffers 15%, dividend yield of 2%.
  1. Tax difference: 15% of the dividend.
  2. Gain: $15\% \times 2\%$ = **30 bp per year**.
- Part goes back to the client as a tighter spread. It is a tax gain on the dividend, **not** a funding benefit.

sections.title: 4. §871(m): US stock, non-US client
sections.body:
- US tax rule. A **dividend equivalent** paid to a non-US person, in a derivative on a US stock, counts as a US-source dividend.
- Withholding: 30%, or the treaty rate.
- Why it exists: before, a swap delivered the US dividend to a foreigner **without withholding**. That was the tax advantage of the swap. The rule closed it.
- Today, a delta one swap on a US stock withholds like the physical stock.
- Scope **today**: only **delta one** transactions, issued since 2017.
- Deferred: the broader test of the final rule (delta ≥ 0.8 at issuance). IRS Notice 2026-61 keeps non-delta-one transactions out **until the end of 2028**. It was the sixth deferral.
- A price return swap does **not** escape: the price embeds the expected dividend, and this implicit dividend counts.
- Exceptions exist, such as qualified indices.
- **QDD** (qualified derivatives dealer): the dealer takes on the withholding on what it pays to the client. In exchange, it suffers no withholding on the dividend it receives as a hedger. This avoids cascading tax along the chain.

sections.title: 5. Special dividends
sections.body:
- An extraordinary dividend is usually treated as an **adjustment event**, not as a dividend flow.
- The adjustment goes to the notional, the strike or the index divisor.
- The confirm or the index rule defines "extraordinary". Read it: it is a common source of breaks between desk and client.
- Practical effect: the DPR may not apply to this payment.

sections.title: 6. The dividend market
sections.body:
- **Index dividend future**: pays the sum of gross ordinary dividends, in index points, with ex-date inside the contract year. E.g.: Euro Stoxx 50.
- It isolates dividend risk from price risk.
- Who ends up long dividends unintentionally: **structured products** desks. The delta hedge of notes linked to price return (autocallables) gains when realized dividends exceed the priced ones, and loses when dividends fall.
- They hedge by **selling** dividend futures or swaps. Delta One is the natural counterparty.
- Dividends implied in an index future (simple interest):
$$D = S(1 + rT) - F$$
- Example: index 5000, financing of 5%, 3-month future at 5040.
  1. $5000 \times 1.0125 = 5062.5$.
  2. $D = 5062.5 - 5040$ = **22.5 points** (future value).
- With known financing, the future reveals dividends. With known dividends, it reveals financing.

sections.title: 7. Where I get confused
sections.body:
- The **ex-date** decides the dividend, not the record date or the pay date.
- DPR applies to the **gross** dividend. DPR of 100% with withholding at source = certain loss for the desk.
- The dividend P&L uses the tax the **desk** suffers, not the client's.
- NTR uses the index provider's rate, not the investor's rate.
- NTR gain is tax, not funding.
- §871(m): price return does not escape. And the current scope is only delta one; the 0.8 test is deferred.
- A higher dividend pushes down the forward and the future. An inverted sign is a common error.
- A special dividend may not go through the DPR.

d1-03-dividendos.summary:
### Dates
- Ex-date decides who receives; the price falls ≈ dividend. Swap: fixes on the ex-date, pays on the pay date.
### Desk
$$\text{P\&L} = D \times (1 - t) - D \times \text{DPR}$$
- E.g.: $2.00 \times 85\% - 2.00 = -0.30$. Fix: DPR = net rate, or spread.
### Indices
- PR: price only. GTR: gross dividend. NTR: net at the provider's rate.
- NTR gain = (provider rate − real rate) × yield. E.g.: $15\% \times 2\%$ = 30 bp.
### §871(m)
- Dividend equivalent to a non-US person = US dividend. Withhold 30% or treaty.
- Today: only delta one. Non-delta-one: out until 2028 (Notice 2026-61).
- Price return does not escape. QDD avoids cascading withholding.
### Market
- Structured desks are long dividends → they sell dividend futures.
- $D = S(1 + rT) - F$.

questions.stem: Explain where the desk's dividend risk comes from in a TRS with a physical hedge, and give two ways to fix it.
questions.answer: The desk receives the dividend net of withholding tax and pays the client the gross dividend times the DPR. questions.stem: Why did §871(m) change non-US clients' demand for swaps on US stocks?
questions.answer: Before the rule, a swap delivered the economics of the US dividend with no tax withheld, while the physical stock suffered 30% or the treaty rate. sections.title: 1. The dates
sections.body:
- **Announcement**: the provider publishes the change.
- **Effective date**: the change applies from the close of the previous trading session.
- Between the two dates, the **pro-forma** composition is known. Everybody plans.
- S&P: quarterly rebalance after the close of the **third Friday** of March, June, September and December.
- MSCI: reviews in February, May, August and November. Announcement about three weeks before; effective near the end of the month.
- MSCI example: November 2026 review → announcement on 11 Nov, effective on 1 Dec. Execution is at the close of 30 Nov.
- The exact dates change every cycle. Use the published calendar.
- Off-calendar events: M&A (deletion when the deal closes), spin-off, IPO with fast entry, change in share count or free float. These can come with little notice.

sections.title: 2. When the tracker must trade
sections.body:
- **Cap-weighted** index: the weight moves with the price, and so does your portfolio. It rebalances itself.
- So a price move does **not** generate a trade. Only these generate trades:
  1. Composition change (addition, deletion).
  2. Share count change (buyback, issuance).
  3. Free-float change.
- **Free-float factor** = fraction of shares available to the public. The weight uses float-adjusted shares. The float changed → the weight changed, with no addition or deletion.
- **Equal-weight** index: the weights drift with price. At each rebalance, the tracker sells the stocks that went up and buys the stocks that went down.
- Consequence: more turnover than a cap-weighted index, and a predictable flow.

sections.title: 3. Why at the close, and who is there
sections.body:
- The index and client swaps use the **official closing price**.
- A tracker wants zero error against this price. So it executes at this price.
- Who shows up at the close of an event:
  1. Passive funds and ETFs (tracking error against the close).
  2. Desks that hedge swaps and index futures.
  3. Active managers and arbitrageurs who positioned early.
  4. Liquidity providers who absorb the auction imbalance.
- In the example: the client swap will be marked at the close. Buying 1 million shares at this price takes the desk's risk to zero.

sections.title: 4. The closing auction
sections.body:
- Orders accumulate before the close. The exchange calculates **one price** that maximizes matched volume.
- All matched orders execute at this price. It becomes the official close.
- **MOC** (market-on-close): executes at the close, at any price.
- **LOC** (limit-on-close): executes at the close only if the price respects the limit.
- From **15:50** (New York time), NYSE and Nasdaq publish the imbalance: matched volume and the excess of buys or sells.
- Cut-off times:
  1. **NYSE**: MOC and LOC until 15:50. After that, only orders that offset a published imbalance.
  2. **Nasdaq**: MOC until 15:55. LOC until 15:58, with possible price adjustment.
- Rule of thumb: a closing order goes in **before** the cut-off. After the cut-off, you can only help the missing side.

sections.title: 5. Restrike risk
sections.body:
- Restrike = the difference between the desk's execution price and the official close.
- Everything that goes to the auction executes at the close: zero restrike.
- What executes before the auction carries the difference:
$$\text{P\&L} = Q_{\text{early}} \times (P_{\text{close}} - P_{\text{avg}})$$
- The formula is for a **buy**. $Q_{\text{early}}$ = quantity executed before the auction.
- Example: buy 1 million. The desk buys 300k before the auction, at an average of 50.40. The close prints at 50.00.
  1. 700k in the auction: no restrike.
  2. 300k before: $300{,}000 \times (50.00 - 50.40)$ = **−USD 120k**.
- For a sale, the sign flips: selling early below the close is a loss.
- The trade-off:
  1. More in the auction → more impact on the close itself.
  2. More before → less impact, more restrike.
- How to size it: the early part depends on the expected auction depth and on the stock's volatility until the close.
- **Guaranteed close**: the desk guarantees the client the official close on a basket. The client gets zero error; the desk takes the execution risk and charges for it.

sections.title: 6. The index effect
sections.body:
- A stock that enters tends to rise between the announcement and the effective date: anticipators buy.
- After the effective date, it usually gives back part of the gain.
- Deletions show the mirror pattern.
- For a tracker, this is a cost: it buys at the peak. For an anticipator, it is a risk: the move may not come, or may reverse early.

sections.title: 7. Index arbitrage and ETFs
sections.body:
- **Index arbitrage**: future against the basket, when the future moves away from fair value.
  1. Rich future: buy the basket, sell the future (cash-and-carry).
  2. Cheap future: the opposite.
- **ETF creation and redemption**: authorized participants (APs) exchange baskets for ETF shares with the fund.
  1. ETF above NAV: the AP buys the basket, delivers it to the fund, receives new ETF shares and sells them. The price falls.
  2. ETF below NAV: the AP buys ETF shares, redeems them, receives the basket and sells it. The price rises.
- Both mechanisms tie a traded price to the value of the underlying basket. The difference is the instrument: a future with an expiry, or an ETF share with no expiry.

sections.title: 8. Leveraged ETFs: the closing flow
sections.body:
- The fund promises $L$ times the **daily** return. It must end each day with exposure = $L$ × assets.
- Rebalance order at the close:
$$\text{order} = A \cdot L \cdot (L-1) \cdot r$$
- $A$ = fund assets, $r$ = index return on the day. The sign follows the market.
- Example: 3x, 1 billion, +2% → exposure 3.06; assets 1.06; target 3.18 → **buy 120 million**.
- Multiplier $L(L-1)$: 2x → 2; 3x → 6; −1x → 2; −2x → 6; −3x → 12. Long and inverse funds trade on the same side: the flows add up.
- Creations and redemptions: add $L$ × net flow. This term follows the investor, not the market.
- Who sends the order: the dealer that hedges the fund's swap.
- Round trip, index 100 → 110 → 100, 2x fund:
  1. Day 1: +20% → 120. The fund buys 20 at the close, at 110.
  2. Day 2: the index falls 9.09% (10/110). The fund falls 18.18% → **98.18**.
  3. The loss of 1.82 is what the 20 bought at the top lost.
- Rule of thumb for the loss on a round trip: $L(L-1) \cdot r^2$.

sections.title: 9. Where I get confused
sections.body:
- The effective date is the next day. The trade is at the **close of the day before**.
- A cap-weighted index needs no trade when the price moves. An equal-weight index does.
- A float change moves the weight with no addition or deletion.
- MOC has no limit price. LOC can simply fail to execute.
- The NYSE and Nasdaq cut-offs differ: 15:50 and 15:55.
- Restrike comes only from the part executed **outside** the auction.
- Restrike sign: bought early above the close = loss; sold early above the close = gain.
- Putting everything in the auction makes restrike zero, but can move the close against you.

d1-04-eventos-indice.summary:

- ETF above NAV: AP creates and sells. Below NAV: AP buys and redeems.

questions.stem: Explain restrike risk and the trade-off between executing early and executing in the auction.

d1-06-mapa-mesas.title: Map of the desks and of funding
d1-06-mapa-mesas.source: SEC Rule 15c3-3 (17 CFR 240.15c3-3); lecture notes (Learn Anything, Delta One). Generic description of a bank; it does not describe any specific institution
d1-06-mapa-mesas.intro:
Student notes. Running example: the **10 million TRS** from the other notes. Here the question is different: which desks and functions does this trade pass through inside a bank?
The map is generic. Each bank organizes them differently.

objectives.text: what each equities desk does
agency and risk; cash PB and synthetic prime
the collateral reuse limit (rehypothecation)
who consumes and who supplies funding, and the role of FTP
which desk or function owns a problem

sections.title: 1. Execution: cash and program trading
sections.body:
- **Cash equities**: executes client orders in stocks.
  1. High touch: with a sales trader.
  2. Low touch: algorithms and direct market access (DMA).
- It is almost all **agency**: the bank executes on behalf of the client. Little risk on the book.
- **Program trading**: baskets. This is where the **risk bid** appears.
- Risk bid: the desk buys or sells the client's whole basket at a guaranteed price (e.g., the close minus a discount). The risk moves to the desk's book, and the desk unwinds it later.
- Agency vs risk: in agency, the price is the market price and the risk is the client's. In risk, the price is guaranteed and the risk is the bank's.

sections.title: 2. Delta One and the strats
sections.body:
- **Delta One** trades: client swaps (single stock, index, custom baskets), futures and index arbitrage, ETFs, financing and dividends.
- Hedges: internalization, physical stock, swap with a dealer, futures and options.
- The product the desk sells is **financing and access**, wrapped in linear exposure.
- **Strats**: build the desk's models, pricing, risk tools and software; analyze flow and P&L.
- They sit with the traders. They are not a separate research unit.
- In the example: the 10 million TRS starts here. Delta One chooses the hedge route and carries the cost.

sections.title: 3. Prime brokerage
sections.body:
- **Prime brokerage** serves hedge funds: it finances longs (margin loans), locates stock for shorts, and provides custody, clearing and reporting.
- **Cash PB**: the client owns the shares, financed by a margin loan.
- **Synthetic prime**: the client holds portfolio swaps; the bank owns the hedges. It overlaps with Delta One.
- Same economics; different balance sheet, legal and tax treatment.
- **Rehypothecation**: the PB reuses the shares pledged as margin (lends them or repos them). This makes client financing cheaper.
- US limit (SEC Rule 15c3-3): the PB can reuse up to **140% of the client's debit balance**. Anything above that is "excess margin" and stays segregated.
- Example: portfolio of 250k, debit balance of 80k.
  1. Reusable: $140\% \times 80$ = **112k**.
  2. Segregated: 250 − 112 = 138k.

sections.title: 4. Stock loan and the bank's inventory
sections.body:
- **Stock loan / sec lending**: sources stock for short sellers.
- Sources: **agent lenders** (custodians that lend on behalf of pension funds and asset managers) and internal inventory.
- Lends to clients and to internal desks. Manages fees, recalls and collateral.
- **Firm-wide inventory management**: match internal longs (desk hedges, PB margin collateral) with internal shorts **before** borrowing externally.
- Why: borrowing internally is cheaper and frees balance sheet.
- In the example: the stock that Delta One bought as a hedge becomes supply for a PB client's short. The lending fee offsets part of the cost of the physical hedge.

sections.title: 5. Volatility and structured products
sections.body:
- **Flow vol**: makes markets in vanilla options (listed and OTC). Carries vol, skew and term-structure risk.
- What it needs from Delta One: borrow cost and dividend forecasts (the forward inputs), and execution of its delta hedges.
- **Exotics / structured products**: designs and hedges notes and exotic options (e.g., autocallables).
- Carries long-dated risk: vol, dividends and correlation.
- It is usually long dividends, and sells this risk. Delta One is a natural counterparty.

sections.title: 6. The funding circuit
sections.body:
- **Treasury / ALM** owns funding and liquidity: issuance, repo strategy, liquidity ratios (LCR, NSFR) and the internal **FTP** curve.
- **Funding consumers**: those who carry long inventory. Delta One hedges, PB margin loans.
- **Funding suppliers**: those who bring cash. Structured note issuance, client short proceeds, deposits.
- Treasury nets them against each other and charges or credits each desk through FTP.
- Why a **structured note** is funding: the investor pays today and the bank repays at maturity. Economically, the bank is borrowing. The investor takes the bank's credit risk.
- The spread on this issuance is usually lower than on plain unsecured debt.
- In the example: the cash that finances the 10 million of stock may come from a note that the structured products desk issued. The two desks complement each other, and FTP is the price between them.

sections.title: 7. Who prices adjustments and who controls
sections.body:
- **XVA**: prices and hedges derivative valuation adjustments, and charges the desks.
  1. CVA: counterparty credit risk.
  2. FVA: funding cost of uncollateralized derivatives.
  3. KVA: capital cost.
  4. MVA: initial margin cost.
- **Product control**: official P&L, valuation and independent price verification.
- **Market risk**: limits, VaR and stress tests.
- Both are independent of the desk. The desk does not mark its own P&L alone.

sections.title: 8. Where I get confused
sections.body:
- Cash equities is agency. A risk bid is risk. Do not mix them.
- Cash PB: the client owns the stock. Synthetic prime: the bank owns it.
- The 140% limit applies to the **debit balance**, not to the portfolio value.
- Stock loan borrows **inside** the bank first, then outside.
- A structured note **supplies** funding. A long Delta One book **consumes** it.
- FTP is not a market cost: it is Treasury's internal price.
- XVA charges adjustments; product control verifies prices; risk sets limits. These are three different owners.
- A strat is not research: the strat sits on the desk.

d1-06-mapa-mesas.summary:
### Desks
- Cash: agency (high/low touch). Program trading: risk bid on baskets.
- Delta One: swaps, futures, ETFs, financing, dividends. Strats sit on the desk.
- PB: margin, borrow, custody. Cash PB (client owns) vs synthetic prime (bank owns).
- Stock loan: agent lenders + internal inventory. Inside before outside.
- Flow vol: vanilla options. Structured: notes, exotics; long dividends.
### Rehypothecation
- Reuse up to 140% of the debit balance (SEC 15c3-3). E.g.: $140\% \times 80$ = 112.
### Funding
- Consumes: long inventory (Delta One, PB margin).
- Supplies: structured notes, client shorts, deposits.
- Treasury nets and charges through FTP.
### Control
- XVA: CVA, FVA, KVA, MVA. Product control: P&L and prices. Risk: limits and VaR.

options.t: Who owns the shares: the client in cash PB, the bank in synthetic prime.
options.why: The economics are the same. The balance sheet, legal and tax treatment change.

questions.stem: What does the flow vol desk need from Delta One to price a single-stock option?

options.t: Borrow cost, dividend forecasts and the delta hedge.
options.why: Borrow and dividends set the forward; Delta One also executes the delta hedge. Vol and skew belong to the vol desk itself.

questions.stem: Delta One increases its physical hedge inventory by 500 million. What happens in the funding circuit?

options.t: The desk consumes more funding, and Treasury charges it through FTP.
options.why: Long inventory needs cash. FTP passes on the cost of debt and balance sheet.

options.t: The desk starts to supply funding.
options.why: Funding suppliers bring cash, for example notes or client shorts.
SOFR cancels out in the swap P&L. The inventory still needs financing.
