questions.stem: Explain how structured notes and Delta One complement each other inside the bank, and the role of Treasury.
questions.answer: The structured note brings cash: the investor pays today and the bank repays at maturity, so the structured products desk supplies funding. Delta One carries long hedge inventory and needs cash, so it consumes funding. Treasury nets the two sides internally and uses FTP to credit the supplier and charge the consumer.

questions.stem: What is rehypothecation, why does it exist, and what is the US limit?
questions.answer: It is the prime broker's reuse of the shares that the client pledged as margin: lending them or repoing them. It exists because it makes client financing cheaper and provides stock for stock loan. In the US, SEC Rule 15c3-3 limits reuse to 140% of the client's debit balance. Anything above that is excess margin and stays segregated.

prob-01-bayes-dice.title: Bayes' theorem: the two-dice casino
prob-01-bayes-dice.source: Casino dice puzzle (Nov 2026); derivation worked in chat; every number checked by running it (posterior formulas, value iteration on |d| ≤ 80)
prob-01-bayes-dice.intro:
Student notes. One example runs to the end: a casino has **two dice that look the same**. One is fair. The other rolls 1–5 with equal chance and never rolls a 6. You pick one at random.
Roll: costs 1 USD; a 6 pays 20 USD and ends the game. Switch: costs 5 USD. Quit: free.
Question of the note: how much does a run of misses tell you, and when should you switch?

objectives.text: prior, likelihood, evidence and posterior, and how they fit in Bayes' theorem
the posterior that a die is fair after a run of misses, with equal or unequal priors
why equal priors cancel and why the face that shows (1 to 5) carries no information
the chance of a 6 on the next roll and the one-roll update of the posterior
why the state reduces to one integer d, and how the Bellman equation is built
why the optimal policy keeps rolling when the immediate expected value is negative

sections.title: 1. The game and the two hypotheses
sections.body:
- Call the dice A and B. Exactly one is fair. Two hypotheses:
  1. $H_A$: A is fair, B is rigged.
  2. $H_B$: B is fair, A is rigged.
- You picked at random → **prior** $P(H_A) = P(H_B) = 1/2$.
- Rigged die: faces 1–5, each 1/5. Fair die: faces 1–6, each 1/6.
- A 6 ends the game. So while you play, every roll you see is a **miss** (1 to 5).
- Assumption: the 20 USD is gross. The 1 USD for that roll is already paid.

sections.title: 2. Bayes' theorem: the four pieces
sections.body:
$$P(H \mid D) = \frac{P(D \mid H)\,P(H)}{P(D)}$$
- $P(H)$ = **prior**: belief in $H$ before the data.
- $P(D \mid H)$ = **likelihood**: how probable the data are if $H$ is true.
- $P(D)$ = **evidence**: how probable the data are overall.
- $P(H \mid D)$ = **posterior**: belief in $H$ after the data.
- The evidence comes from the law of total probability (sum over all hypotheses):
$$P(D) = P(D \mid H_A)P(H_A) + P(D \mid H_B)P(H_B)$$
- Its job: make the posteriors of all hypotheses sum to 1.

sections.title: 3. Likelihood: only the miss count matters
sections.body:
- Data: $a$ misses on A, $b$ misses on B.
- Chance of one specific face (say a 3):
  1. fair die: 1/6
  2. rigged die: 1/5
- Ratio per miss: $(1/6)/(1/5) = 5/6$, **for every face**. → the face value adds nothing. Only the count matters.
- So, counting misses only:
  1. $P(D \mid H_A) = (5/6)^a \cdot 1^b$ (A fair misses with 5/6 each time; B rigged always misses)
  2. $P(D \mid H_B) = 1^a \cdot (5/6)^b$
- Example: $a = 2$, $b = 0$ → $P(D \mid H_A) = 25/36 \approx 0.694$; $P(D \mid H_B) = 1$.

sections.title: 4. The posterior, step by step
sections.body:
1. Plug in:
$$P(H_A \mid D) = \frac{(5/6)^a \cdot \tfrac12}{(5/6)^a \cdot \tfrac12 + (5/6)^b \cdot \tfrac12}$$
2. The 1/2 is in every term → it cancels. (Only because the priors are equal.)
$$P(H_A \mid D) = \frac{(5/6)^a}{(5/6)^a + (5/6)^b}$$
3. Divide top and bottom by $(5/6)^a$:
$$P(H_A \mid D) = \frac{1}{1 + (6/5)^{a-b}}$$
- The evidence did **not** disappear. It is the whole denominator.
- Only $a - b$ matters.
- Example $a = 2$, $b = 0$: evidence $= 0.694 \times 0.5 + 1 \times 0.5 = 0.847$ → posterior $= 0.347 / 0.847 \approx$ **0.410**. Formula: $1/(1 + 1.2^2) = 1/2.44 \approx 0.410$. Same.
- Odds form (same thing, shorter): posterior odds = prior odds × likelihood ratio. Here odds$(H_A) = 1 \times (5/6)^{a-b}$. For $a - b = 2$: $0.694$ → $0.694/1.694 = 0.410$.
- Unequal prior, e.g. $P(H_A) = 0.8$, $a = 2$, $b = 0$: $0.8 \times 0.694 / (0.8 \times 0.694 + 0.2) = 0.556/0.756 \approx$ **0.735**. The prior no longer cancels.

sections.title: 5. One roll at a time
sections.body:
- $q$ = P(the die in hand is fair).
- Chance of a 6 on the next roll (total probability again):
$$P(6) = q \cdot \tfrac16 + (1-q) \cdot 0 = \tfrac{q}{6}$$
- After a miss, today's posterior is tomorrow's prior:
$$q' = \frac{q \cdot \tfrac56}{q \cdot \tfrac56 + (1-q)} = \frac{5q}{6-q}$$
- Example: $q = 0.5$ → $q' = 2.5/5.5 = 5/11 \approx$ **0.455**.
- Check: $1/(1 + 1.2^1) = 0.455$. One-at-a-time = all-at-once. (Checked for every $d$ from −20 to 20.)
- Example: $q = 0.410$ → $P(6) = 0.410/6 \approx$ **0.068**, not 1/6.

sections.title: 6. The state: one integer d
sections.body:
- Take the die in hand as the reference.
- $d$ = (misses of the die in hand) − (misses of the other die).
$$q(d) = \frac{1}{1 + (6/5)^d}$$
- P(other die is fair) = $1 - q(d)$, because exactly one is fair.
- Moves:
  1. Roll, miss → $d \to d + 1$.
  2. Switch → the other die becomes the reference → $d \to -d$.
- Start: $d = 0$, $q = 0.5$.
- Table: $q(2) = 0.410$; $q(5) = 0.287$; $q(8) = 0.189$; $q(9) = 0.162$.

sections.title: 7. The decision: Bellman equation and result
sections.body:
- $V(d)$ = best expected profit from state $d$. Three choices, take the max:
$$V(d) = \max\Big\{\, 0,\; -1 + \tfrac{q}{6} \cdot 20 + \big(1 - \tfrac{q}{6}\big) V(d+1),\; -5 + V(-d) \,\Big\}$$
  1. 0 = quit.
  2. Roll: pay 1; with $q/6$ win 20 and stop; else go to $d + 1$.
  3. Switch: pay 5; go to $-d$.
- Answer to the puzzle = $V(0)$ and the choice that reaches it.
- Solved by value iteration on $|d| \le 80$:
  1. Roll while $d \le 8$. Switch at $d = 9$ ($q = 0.162$).
  2. After the switch: $d = -9$, so the new die has $q = 0.838$.
  3. Never quit. $V(0) \approx$ **3.634 USD**.
- Immediate value of a roll: $20q/6 - 1 > 0$ only if $q > 0.3$. That is $d \le 4$.
- At $d = 5$ to $8$ ($q$ from 0.287 to 0.189) a roll loses money on average, but the optimum still rolls. → each miss is **information**: it makes the switch safer.

sections.title: 8. Where I get confused
sections.body:
- The prior cancels **only** because both priors are 1/2.
- The evidence $P(D)$ never disappears. It is the denominator, written out.
- Forgetting the denominator: $(5/6)^a$ alone is a likelihood, not a posterior.
- The face (1, 2, …, 5) is not extra data: every face has ratio 5/6.
- $P(6)$ is $q/6$, not $1/6$. You do not know the die is fair.
- $q$ is about the die in hand. The other die is fair with $1 - q$.
- Switching flips $d$ to $-d$. It does not reset it to 0.
- Negative immediate value ≠ stop. The future (switching with better information) counts.

prob-01-bayes-dice.summary:
### Bayes
- $P(H \mid D) = P(D \mid H)\,P(H) / P(D)$
- $P(D) = \sum_i P(D \mid H_i) P(H_i)$
- Odds form: posterior odds = prior odds × likelihood ratio.
### The dice
- Ratio per miss = 5/6 (any face). Only the miss count matters.
- $q(d) = 1/(1 + (6/5)^d)$, $d$ = misses in hand − misses other.
- E.g. $d = 2$ → 0.410; $d = 9$ → 0.162.
- One roll: $q' = 5q/(6-q)$; $P(6) = q/6$.
### Decision
- $V(d) = \max\{0,\; -1 + \tfrac{q}{6} 20 + (1-\tfrac{q}{6}) V(d+1),\; -5 + V(-d)\}$
- Roll while $d \le 8$; switch at $d = 9$; never quit. $V(0) \approx 3.634$ USD.
- Myopic roll value > 0 only if $q > 0.3$; the optimum rolls further (information).

questions.stem: Equal priors. Die A missed 3 times; die B was never rolled. What is P(A is fair)?

options.why: That is $(5/6)^3$, the likelihood alone. It is not normalized by the evidence.
That is $(5/6)^3 \times 0.5$, the numerator. The evidence in the denominator is missing.
Misses are evidence: a rigged die always misses, a fair one only 5/6 of the time.

questions.stem: Equal priors. A missed 4 times, then you switched and B missed 2 times. What is P(A is fair)?

options.why: Only $a - b = 2$ matters: $1/(1 + 1.2^2) \approx 0.410$.
That uses $a = 4$ and ignores B's misses. B's misses are evidence that B is rigged, so A gains.
That treats all 6 misses as evidence against A: $1/(1 + 1.2^6)$.
That is $q(-2)$: P(B is fair), the other die.

questions.stem: In the posterior $(5/6)^a / [(5/6)^a + (5/6)^b]$, why is there no $P(H_A)$?

options.t: Both priors are 1/2, so the factor is in every term and cancels.
options.why: With unequal priors it stays in the formula.

options.t: The evidence $P(D)$ equals 1, so Bayes reduces to the likelihood.
options.why: $P(D)$ is the denominator, written out. It is not 1 (e.g. 0.847 for $a = 2$, $b = 0$).

options.t: After enough rolls the data dominate, so the prior does not matter.
options.why: True in the limit, but the prior cancels here exactly, for any number of rolls.

options.t: The prior only matters for continuous parameters.
options.why: Bayes' theorem uses the prior for discrete hypotheses too.

questions.stem: You have a tip: P(A is fair) = 0.8 before any roll. A misses twice. What is P(A is fair) now?

options.why: That is the equal-prior answer. With a prior of 0.8 the prior no longer cancels.
That is the numerator $0.8 \times (5/6)^2$. Divide by the evidence.
Two misses are evidence against A. The posterior must fall.

questions.stem: The die in hand has $q = 0.410$. What is the chance that the next roll is a 6?

options.why: 1/6 assumes the die is fair. You only believe that with 0.410.
That is P(fair), not P(6). A fair die still misses 5/6 of the time.
That is $(1-q)/6$: it uses P(rigged), and the rigged die never rolls a 6.

questions.stem: Two players each see one miss on die A. One saw a 3, the other only heard "not a 6". Do their posteriors differ?

options.t: No: for every face, P(face | fair)/P(face | rigged) = (1/6)/(1/5) = 5/6, the same as for "not a 6".
options.why: The face carries no extra information. Only the miss count matters.

options.t: Yes: the player who saw the 3 has more data, so a sharper posterior.
options.why: More detail is not more information here. The likelihood ratio is 5/6 either way.

options.t: Yes: a 3 is more likely on the rigged die (1/5 > 1/6), so it moves the posterior more.
options.why: "Not a 6" has the same ratio: (5/6)/1 = 5/6.

questions.stem: Start with $q = 0.5$. One roll, a miss. What is $q$ now?

options.why: That is $0.5 \times 5/6$: the numerator only. Divide by $0.5 \times 5/6 + 0.5$.
A miss is less likely on the fair die, so the belief in fair must fall.
That is $1 - 0.455$: P(the other die is fair).

questions.stem: The die in hand has 9 misses, the other has 0, so $d = 9$. You switch. What is P(the new die in hand is fair)?

options.why: Switching sends $d \to -9$: $q(-9) = 1 - q(9) = 1 - 0.162 \approx 0.838$.
Switching does not reset $d$ to 0. The 9 misses stay as evidence.
That is P(the old die is fair). Exactly one die is fair, so the new one has $1 - 0.162$.

questions.stem: At $d = 6$, $q = 0.251$. The immediate value of a roll is $20 \times 0.251/6 - 1 \approx -0.16$ USD. What does the optimal policy do?

options.t: Roll: each miss raises the value of switching later, and that outweighs the small loss.
options.why: The optimum rolls up to $d = 8$ and switches at $d = 9$. $V(6) \approx 2.96 > 0$.

options.t: Quit: a roll with negative expected value should never be taken.
options.why: That ignores the future. Quitting gives 0, but $V(6) \approx 2.96$.

options.t: Switch now: once a roll has negative value, switch at once.
options.why: Switch now gives $-5 + V(-6) \approx 2.29$, below roll at 2.96.

questions.stem: Why does the whole history of rolls reduce to one integer $d$, and what are the transitions?
questions.answer: The posterior is $1/(1 + (6/5)^{a-b})$: it depends only on the difference of miss counts. The face values add nothing (ratio 5/6 for every face). Measure it from the die in hand: $d$ = misses in hand − misses other. A miss sends $d \to d+1$; a switch sends $d \to -d$; a 6 or quitting ends the game.

sd-01-scale.title: Scale: capacity, latency and caching
sd-01-scale.source: Little (1961); Harchol-Balter, Performance Modeling and Design of Computer Systems (2013), ch. 6; Dean & Barroso, The Tail at Scale (CACM, 2013); Karger et al., Consistent Hashing (STOC 1997); RFC 9111 (HTTP caching)
sd-01-scale.intro:
Student notes. One example runs to the end: a **link shortener**. A user opens `sho.rt/abc`; the service looks up the long URL and answers with a redirect.
Load: **100 million redirects per day**, peak 5× the average. Reads dominate: a link is created once and opened many times.
Question of the note: how many machines, how much cache, and what breaks first? All numbers are illustrative.

objectives.text: capacity from traffic: requests per second, concurrency (Little's law), utilization and queueing delay
the chance a fan-out request hits a slow server, and why to watch p99
vertical and horizontal scaling, L4 and L7 load balancers, hash mod n and consistent hashing
cache-aside, write-through, write-back and CDN caching
overload: cache stampede, hit-ratio drop, missing back-pressure, rate limits

sections.title: 1. Back-of-envelope numbers
sections.body:
- First step of every design: turn the business number into requests per second.
- A day = 86,400 s ≈ $10^5$ s.
- Example: 100 million / 86,400 ≈ **1,160 req/s** on average.
- Size for the **peak**, not the average. Peak = 5× → ≈ **5,800 req/s**.
- Latency ladder (orders of magnitude, not specs):
  - main-memory read ~100 ns
  - SSD random read ~100 µs
  - round trip, same datacenter ~0.5 ms
  - round trip, cross-continent ~100–150 ms
- Rule: one cross-continent round trip ≈ a million memory reads. Count network round trips first.
- Latency vs throughput:
  - Latency: time for one request.
  - Throughput: requests completed per second.
  - Batching raises throughput and latency together.

sections.title: 2. Little's law and queueing
sections.body:
- **Little's law**: $L = \lambda W$.
  - $L$: requests in the system (in flight).
  - $\lambda$: arrival rate. $W$: time each request spends inside.
  - Holds for any stable system, whatever the arrival pattern.
- Example: peak 5,800 req/s, 50 ms end to end at the server.
  - $L = 5{,}800 \times 0.05 = 290$ requests in flight.
  - → at least 290 concurrent slots (threads, connections, async tasks) across the fleet.
- **Utilization** $\rho$ = busy time / total time.
  - Example: 10 ms of CPU per request → $5{,}800 \times 0.010 = 58$ cores busy at 100%.
- **M/M/1 queue** (one server, random arrivals): $W = \dfrac{S}{1-\rho}$, $S$ = service time.
  - $S$ = 10 ms: $\rho = 0.5$ → 20 ms · $\rho = 0.7$ → 33 ms · $\rho = 0.9$ → 100 ms.
- Latency is not linear in load. From 0.5 to 0.9, load grows 1.8×; latency grows 5×.
- Rough rule: target $\rho \approx 0.7$ at peak → $58 / 0.7 \approx$ **83 cores**.
- M/M/1 is a rough model. Real servers have many workers and less random arrivals. The shape (blow-up near 1) is the lesson.

sections.title: 3. Tail latency and fan-out
sections.body:
- p99 = the latency that 99% of requests beat. The slowest 1% sit above it.
- The average hides the tail. Users who click a lot hit the tail often.
- **Fan-out**: one user request calls $n$ servers in parallel and waits for **all** of them.
  - Each server is slow with probability $p$.
  - P(request slow) = $1 - (1-p)^n$.
- Example: the stats page of a link reads click counts from 20 shards; each shard is slow 1% of the time.
  - $1 - 0.99^{20} \approx$ **18%** of page loads are slow.
  - With 100 shards: $1 - 0.99^{100} \approx 63\%$.
- → in a fan-out, the p99 of one server becomes the median experience.
- Mitigations (Dean & Barroso): hedged requests (send a copy after a short delay, take the first answer), fewer shards per request, timeouts with partial results.

sections.title: 4. Scaling the service tier
sections.body:
- **Vertical**: a bigger machine.
  - Simple: no code change.
  - Capped by the largest machine, and one machine = one point of failure.
- **Horizontal**: more machines behind a load balancer.
  - Needs **stateless** services: any instance can serve any request.
  - State moves out: database, cache, or a signed token on the client.
- Example: the redirect tier is stateless. 83 cores → e.g. 11 machines of 8 cores, plus spares for a failure.
- **Load balancer**:
  - L4: routes by IP and port. Fast. Does not read the request.
  - L7: reads HTTP. Routes by path or header, terminates TLS, retries.
- **Amdahl's law** caps parallel speedup: $\dfrac{1}{(1-p) + p/n}$, $p$ = parallel share, $n$ = cores.
  - Example: a nightly job recounts clicks; 90% of it parallelizes.
  - 10 cores → $1/(0.1 + 0.09) \approx 5.3\times$. Infinite cores → $1/0.1 = 10\times$.
  - The serial 10% sets the ceiling. Shrink it before you buy cores.

sections.title: 5. Caching
sections.body:
- A cache keeps hot data in memory, near the reader. It trades freshness for speed.
- **Cache-aside** (the common default):
  - Read: try the cache → on a miss, read the DB and store the value with a TTL.
  - Write: update the DB → **delete** the key. Do not update it: two racing writers can leave the older value in the cache.
- **Write-through**: the write goes to cache and DB before the acknowledgement. Consistent cache; slower writes.
- **Write-back**: acknowledge after the cache write; flush to the DB later. Fast writes; a cache crash loses unflushed data.
- **Eviction**: LRU removes the least recently used key when the cache is full (hash map + doubly linked list, O(1)).
- **CDN**: caches responses on edge servers near users. Saves the long round trip and origin load. `Cache-Control` and TTLs (RFC 9111) control freshness.
- Example: link lookups are cache-aside, hit ratio 90%. Cache read 1 ms, DB read 20 ms.
  - Mean lookup = $0.9 \times 1 + 0.1 \times (1 + 20) = 3$ ms.
  - DB load at peak = 10% × 5,800 = **580 req/s**.
- The DB sees the **miss** rate. Hit ratio 90% → 80% doubles the DB load (580 → 1,160 req/s).

sections.title: 6. Spreading keys across nodes
sections.body:
- The cache is a cluster. Each key must map to one node.
- **hash(key) mod n**: simple, but adding a node remaps most keys.
  - Example: 4 → 5 cache nodes. A key stays only if $k \bmod 4 = k \bmod 5$: **80% of keys move**.
  - Moved keys are misses → hit ratio falls → the DB takes the load (section 5).
- **Consistent hashing**: nodes and keys sit on a ring; a key belongs to the next node clockwise.
  - Adding a 5th node moves only the keys it takes over: about $1/5$ = **20%**.
  - **Virtual nodes**: each node owns many points on the ring. Evens out the load and the moved share.

sections.title: 7. Overload and protection
sections.body:
- **Cache stampede**: a hot key expires and many requests miss at once → all hit the DB.
  - Example: a viral link with 2,000 req/s; its key expires; every request in the next 20 ms goes to the DB.
  - Fixes: request coalescing (one loader, the others wait), TTL jitter, refresh before expiry.
- **Rate limiting with a token bucket**:
  - The bucket holds up to $b$ tokens and refills at $r$ per second. Each request takes one token or is rejected.
  - Allows bursts up to $b$; long-run average $r$.
  - Example: per-client $b = 100$, $r = 10$/s, bucket full. A burst of 150 → 100 pass, 50 rejected. After 3 s, 30 tokens are back.
- **Back-pressure**: a slow consumer makes producers slow down (bounded queue, blocking, credits).
  - Without it, an unbounded queue grows until memory runs out, and every request waits behind the backlog.
- **Headroom**: from section 2, near $\rho = 1$ latency explodes. Protection keeps the system out of that zone.

sections.title: 8. Confusions to avoid
sections.body:
- Sizing for the average instead of the peak.
- Thinking latency grows linearly with load. Near saturation it explodes ($S/(1-\rho)$).
- Little's law gives **concurrency**, not throughput. $L = \lambda W$, not $\lambda = L W$.
- Watching the average latency. In a fan-out, a rare slow server becomes the common case.
- Updating the cached key on a write. Delete it: deletes are idempotent; racing updates leave stale data.
- Write-back is not "consistent and fast". It is fast, and loses data if the cache dies before the flush.
- A small hit-ratio drop looks harmless. The DB sees the miss rate: 10% → 20% misses = 2× DB load.
- Rescaling a cache with hash mod n. Most keys move at once → miss storm.
- Adding cores past the Amdahl ceiling. The serial part does not shrink.

sd-01-scale.summary:
### Envelope
- req/s ≈ per day / $10^5$. Size for **peak**.
- Memory 100 ns · SSD 100 µs · DC round trip 0.5 ms · cross-continent 100–150 ms.
### Queueing
- Little: $L = \lambda W$ → concurrency.
- M/M/1: $W = S/(1-\rho)$. $\rho$ 0.5 → 2S · 0.9 → 10S. Target ≈ 0.7.
### Tail
- Fan-out to $n$: P(slow) $= 1-(1-p)^n$. 20 × 1% → 18% · 100 × 1% → 63%.
### Scale
- Horizontal needs stateless. L4 = IP/port · L7 = HTTP.
- Amdahl: $1/((1-p)+p/n)$, ceiling $1/(1-p)$.
### Cache
- Aside: app fills; write → update DB, **delete** key.
- Through: consistent, slow writes · Back: fast, can lose data.
- DB load = miss rate × traffic.
### Keys
- mod n: 4→5 moves 80% · consistent hashing ≈ $1/n$.
### Overload
- Stampede → coalesce, jitter TTL, refresh early.
- Token bucket: burst $b$, average $r$. Back-pressure = bounded queues.

questions.stem: The shortener serves 100 million redirects per day. Peak is 5× the average. What peak rate do you size for?

options.why: That is the average. The fleet must survive the peak.
Off by 10×: a day has ~86,400 s, not ~8,640.
That divides by 1,440 (minutes in a day), not by 86,400 seconds.

questions.stem: Peak 5,800 req/s; each request spends 50 ms in the server. How many requests are in flight on average?

options.why: Little's law: $L = \lambda W = 5{,}800 \times 0.05 = 290$.
That would be 20 ms in the system, not 50 ms.
That is $\lambda / W$. Little's law multiplies rate by time.
That is the arrival rate, not the concurrency.

questions.stem: One server behaves like an M/M/1 queue with service time 10 ms. Load rises from $\rho = 0.5$ to $\rho = 0.9$. Mean time in system?

options.why: That assumes latency grows in proportion to load. Queueing delay is not linear.
The service time stays 10 ms, but requests also wait in the queue.
That is $S \times \rho$, the busy time per request slot, not the time in system.

questions.stem: Cache-aside, hit ratio 90%, peak 5,800 req/s. A deploy changes the key format and the hit ratio drops to 80%. What happens to the DB load?

options.why: The DB sees the miss rate: 10% → 20% of 5,800.
11% is the relative drop in hit ratio (90 → 80). The DB load follows the misses.
5,800 × 0.8 is the traffic the cache serves (hits). The DB gets the misses.

options.t: Nothing changes; the cache absorbs it
options.why: Every miss goes to the DB by definition of cache-aside.

questions.stem: The stats page reads 20 shards in parallel and waits for all of them. Each shard is slow 1% of the time, independently. What share of page loads is slow?

options.why: That holds for one shard. The page waits for the slowest of 20.
Close, but adding 20 × 1% overcounts the cases where two shards are slow.
That is the answer for 100 shards.

questions.stem: The cache cluster grows from 4 to 5 nodes with `hash(key) mod n`. Roughly what share of keys moves to a different node?

options.why: A key stays only if $k \bmod 4 = k \bmod 5$: 4 of every 20 values. 80% move, and each moved key is a miss.
That is consistent hashing: the new node takes about $1/5$ of the keys.
That is $1/4$. It is not how mod n remaps.
The node index depends on $n$, so changing $n$ remaps keys.

questions.stem: A nightly job recounts clicks. 90% of it parallelizes. Best speedup with 10 cores, and with unlimited cores?

options.why: That ignores the serial 10%, which every run still pays.
10 cores only reach 10× if the whole job is parallel.
The serial share sets a ceiling of $1/(1-p)$.

questions.stem: Cache-aside. A user edits where a link points. What should the write path do?

options.t: Update the DB, then delete the cached key
options.why: The next read misses and loads the new value. A delete is idempotent; two racing writers cannot leave the older value.

options.t: Update the DB, then write the new value into the cache
options.why: Two concurrent writers can finish in the wrong order and leave the older value cached.

options.t: Write the cache only; a background job flushes to the DB
options.why: That is write-back: fast, but a cache crash loses the edit.

options.t: Do nothing; the TTL will expire the old value
options.why: Users get the wrong redirect until the TTL ends.

questions.stem: A viral link gets 2,000 req/s. Every hour, at the same moment, DB latency spikes for a second, then recovers. Most likely cause?

options.t: Cache stampede: the hot key expires and every request misses at once
options.why: Fix: request coalescing, TTL jitter or refresh before expiry.

options.t: The DB is under-sized for the average load
options.why: Then latency would be high all the time, not in a short spike.

options.t: LRU evicted the key because it was rarely used
options.why: LRU keeps hot keys. The hourly pattern points to a TTL.
Back-pressure protects the DB; it does not create an hourly spike.

questions.stem: Token bucket per client: capacity 100, refill 10 tokens/s, bucket full. The client sends 150 requests at once, then waits 3 s. Result?

options.why: The burst drains the bucket; refill is 10/s × 3 s.

options.t: 150 pass; the average stays under the limit
options.why: A burst can only spend the tokens in the bucket.
That treats the bucket as a fixed 10-per-second window. The bucket allows a burst up to its capacity.

options.t: 100 pass, 50 queued and served over 5 s
options.why: A plain token bucket rejects. Queueing is a leaky-bucket or shaping design.

questions.stem: Compare write-through and write-back caching. When would you accept write-back?
questions.answer: Write-through writes the cache and the DB before the acknowledgement: the cache stays consistent, but each write pays the DB latency. Write-back acknowledges after the cache write and flushes later: writes are fast, but a cache crash loses the unflushed data. Accept write-back only when losing the last few writes is tolerable (counters, metrics, view counts) or the cache itself is durable and replicated.

questions.stem: Explain why a service that calls many backends should watch p99, not the average latency.
questions.answer: The request waits for the slowest backend. With n backends each slow with probability p, the request is slow with probability 1 − (1 − p)^n, which grows fast with n (20 × 1% → 18%). So a rare tail on one backend becomes a common case for users. The average hides that tail; p99 shows it.
